utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Happy new year. And welcome back to this case. We noticed that the successor of Ms. Sinatra is present in this courtroom. For the sake of the record, would you please introduce yourself, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, my name is Branko Lukic and I am representing Mr. Jokic as his co-counsel today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And we also notice that the counsel for Mr. Deronjic is also present in this courtroom. For the sake of the record would you please introduce yourself to the bench. Yes, you have the floor, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am Slobodan Cvijetic and I am the counsel of the accused, Miroslav Deronjic in this case, and I am familiar with my rights aware that I can intervene with legal questions but not as to factual matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So there is no need for me to remind you about that. Before we have the next witness, there are several procedural matters that we have to deal with. The first one is that the Prosecution filed a motion on the 18th December last year asking for dropping six Prosecution witnesses. During the breaks and after consultations with my colleagues, we would like to say that this motion is granted. The next issue is that we believe that we should admit witness 80 under Rule 92 bis without cross-examination. The third matter is that I would like to ask the views from the parties about two 92 bis witnesses in relation to the cross-examination. That was in a motion filed December 5th last year. The first one is Mr. Erdemovic. Mr. Karnavas, I would like to ask you first of all to know whether you still want to cross-examine this witness or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Happy new year. If we were to cross-examine Mr. Erdemovic, we believe this could be accomplished within one or two sessions. It would be limited to one particular matter. I have read all of the statements. I believe that the Prosecutor and I are very close in our interpretation of Mr. Erdemovic's prior testimony. However, Mr. Blagojevic did express his discontent with respect to one aspect where Mr. Erdemovic seems to have been somewhat equivocal. So our cross-examination would be primarily focused on that. So I believe one or two sessions at the very most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. Could I turn to Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I believe the issue is related to whether Mr. Erdemovic suggests in any way that the squad that assisted him at the Branjevo Farm was from the Bratunac Brigade. And as Mr. Karnavas and I have looked through the record and had agreed that he never makes that suggestion, and I have, on his request, have confirmed that for the record. As you recall, Mr. Blagojevic had some concern over that. So we are prepared to stipulate on that. Mr. -- in my view, Mr. Erdemovic has always been very clear and consistent on that point. This Prosecutor will never suggest otherwise. However, I understand Mr. Karnavas's concerns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, even if Mr. Erdemovic mentioned those people from the Bratunac Brigade specifically, but he did not say or indicate in any way that this matter is related to any orders or acknowledgment of your client in this point. So in these circumstances, I believe there is a meeting of minds from both parties on that issue. So do you think there is still a need to cross-examine that witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may give an explanation, as opposed to giving a yes or no answer. The -- Mr. Erdemovic has given many, many different statements and has been questioned on a variety of occasions in different proceedings. And on almost every occasion Mr. Erdemovic has indicated that the soldiers or the people that came to assist in the killings at Branjevo Farm on the morning of I believe it's the 16th were from Bratunac, not the Bratunac Brigade. There were some leading questions at one point that would perhaps leave to the suggestion that Mr. Erdemovic was conceding at some point that they might have been from the Bratunac Brigade. That's the very narrow issue. In my opinion, a close reading of Mr. Erdemovic's testimony clearly indicates that at no time he states that they were from the Bratunac Brigade. I believe Mr. McCloskey on the record now is conceding the point, or acknowledging the point I should say because I don't think there was ever -- the Prosecution has never argued that Erdemovic has, in fact, stated that they were from the Bratunac Brigade, and in fact we had Mr. Butler indicate that as well on the record. So I think the record is quite clear. Also, there is additional testimony from other witnesses that would shed light as to who might have participated, and of course would be helpful to the Trial Chamber in making its findings of facts. In light of that, in my professional opinion, I believe that there would be no need to bring Mr. Erdemovic. However, irrespective of how I, as a professional, may feel, Mr. Blagojevic may be of a different opinion. And given my position as counsel, on this particular issue it would appear that I would need to follow the instructions of my client, which would be Mr. Blagojevic. So if Mr. Blagojevic insists on having Mr. Erdemovic over here, then that would be my position, that I would make that request and then leave it to the Court's discretion to make their determination. On the other hand, if the Court were to make a finding of fact at this point, that based on the stipulation or based on the remarks by the Prosecution and the Defence, the Trial Chamber will indeed make a finding of fact that those members were not from the Bratunac Brigade or at least there's no evidence to suggest that from the Bratunac Brigade, pursuant to Mr. Erdemovic's testimony. In other words, there may be some other evidence out there yet to come from which the Court could reach their decision. But I believe, at least with respect to Erdemovic's testimony, then I think that would eliminate the need of bringing Mr. Erdemovic back, because I understand there are some complications given that he is under the witness protection program and there's a lot of logistical issues and -- and again, as I indicated, his testimony would take probably one session, two at the very most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much, Mr. Karnavas. As for this specific issue, I believe that there is a meeting of minds between the two parties of this particular issue, and if there is some areas which is equivocal or unclear, this Bench will interpret the testimony of the witness in favour of the accused, which means that the Prosecution has to present the evidence beyond reasonable doubt to incriminalise the accused. So on this particular matter and concerning with this particular witness, this Bench believes that we don't need the cross-examination of this witness. As for the next witness, her name is Ibrahimafendic. On the 17th of December last year, Mr. Karnavas expressed a view that he would like to cross-examine her and he might have some reasons for that. At that time, we hoped Mr. Karnavas could reconsider his positions on this issue. If you insist, Mr. Karnavas, would you please tell us the concrete reasons for doing that. Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. With all due respect, if I could ask for the Court's indulgence for -- to come back to the Court tomorrow on that. In light of the Court's specific instructions, I would like to be very careful and re-examine my position and be very specific in the event I do wish to continue with my previous request. So if I could have one day, Your Honour, and address this issue tomorrow, I would very much appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Are there any other matters that the parties would like to bring to the attention of this Bench? Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If we could go into private session just for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There is a technical matter here. Apparently, Ms. Tomanovic's ear -- well, it says she has no acoustics --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I'm afraid I'm unable to assist in these technical matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. I'm sorry that we have kept you waiting for a long time, but you have to understand that at the beginning of a year, there are a lot of housekeeping matters to deal with. Are you ready to start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, Your Honour. Yes, I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Mr. McCloskey, your direct examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you for the record give us your name and spell your last name.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: My name is Miroslav Deronjic, D -- rather M-i-r-o-s-l-a-v, D-e-r-o-n-j-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And as you know, I'll have just a few questions for you this morning, pursuant to the Court process. And I want to ask you about, to start off, just a few documents. But is it not true that you are testifying today here pursuant to a plea agreement that you entered into with the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you pled guilty in an indictment that related to the May 9th attack and burning of the village of Glogova in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where I believe at least 65 Muslims were killed, murdered in that attack?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Mr. President, we have marked that the plea agreement and the factual basis with 689, and I don't believe we need to go any further than that. And the B/C/S version is I believe as we usually -- just 689(B).

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go now to 11 July 1995, where you have previously said you were at Pribicevac I believe in the afternoon hours. Can you tell us, did you have any contact with Mr. Blagojevic at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I said in my statement that during the Srebrenica operation, I had first seen Mr. Blagojevic on the 11th. It was a brief accidental encounter at Pribicevac. At the time, the Army of Republika Srpska had received an order to enter the town of Srebrenica. We met and spent five to six minutes talking. That was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did Mr. Blagojevic say to you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: It was an ordinary conversation. We exchanged our information as to the ending of the Srebrenica information -- operation. And I think that at one point we set out together in the direction of Srebrenica; however, shortly after that I received invitation to return to Bratunac. So that is why I didn't see Mr. Blagojevic after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know if Mr. Blagojevic's troops were doing anything relating to that -- to Srebrenica, or whether he said anything about what his troops were doing?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that the forces of the Bratunac Brigade were deployed along that line, and at Pribicevac in those days I had an opportunity of visiting some of the units deployed in the area. But at that moment, when I encountered Mr. Blagojevic, the units were on the move towards Srebrenica. They had received an order to enter Srebrenica, and the units under Mr. Blagojevic's command were carrying out that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me briefly ask you about something you said to Mr. Jean Rene Ruez, who I'm sure you remember. You've provided several statements to the Office of the Prosecutor prior to your arrest, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And on February 4, 1998, you mentioned to Mr. Ruez that you had gone to Pale and spoken to the president on the 11th and 12th of July, and that upon your return you called a meeting with General Mladic and some civilian representatives, as well at the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, what you identified as Mr. Blagojevic. Now, since that particular statement, you have not mentioned such a meeting. Can you tell us today whether what you told Mr. Ruez on February 4th, 1998, was correct or not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: No. This was not correct. I did not correctly convey the information as regards the events taking place in the evening of the 11th, or rather, starting on the evening of the 11th and then going on for the next couple of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you briefly explain that, why you were not correctly relating the events when you met with Mr. Ruez.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: There's several reasons for that, Mr. McCloskey. Let me just mention the most important ones. That was my first encounter with an investigator of the OTP. I had been informed by an official of the government of Republika Srpska that I should appear at Pale and give a statement relating to the events this Srebrenica. So I was not fully informed as to the contents of the conversation that was supposed to take place at Pale. Of course it was a surprise -- this invitation came as a surprise, and it was the first such invitation and it was only then that I realised that I was interesting for the investigators of the OTP. So I came to Pale. I gave a statement, and then another one in the premises of the government of Republika Srpska. Those statements were given in very complex circumstances. When I say "complex circumstances," I'm referring both to political circumstances and a general atmosphere and climate, as regards the political leadership of Republika Srpska and their attitude towards the Tribunal. I'm also referring to the security issues, because the very fact that I gave this statement in the premises of the government of Republika Srpska imply the possibility for such statements to be distributed or sent to various addressees, the addressees that I didn't think would be favourable to me. I tried to present the facts as regards the events in Srebrenica, but at the same time I wanted to avoid mentioning the facts that were directly related to the leadership of Republika Srpska when it comes to these events. And that is the main reason for the discrepancies between those statements, the statements that I gave at that time, and the statement that I gave later on to the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So does that mean that some of your statements regarding the leadership of Republika Srpska, such as Radovan Karadzic, were deliberately not true in order to --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did that regard -- also regarding your involvement in some of the Srebrenica events. Were you completely truthful about your involvement?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: You mean in the last -- during the last interview or are you referring to the first interviews?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The first interviews prior to your beginning to enter into plea negotiations with the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Well, both facts that I omitted to mention in those statements are related to me, including the encounter with President Karadzic and the implications of that encounter. So the answer is yes, I'm directly related to those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. You understand Mr. Karnavas is, and perhaps the Judges are going to be asking you questions specifically about many of those statements?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You understand that I will not be?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, if we -- we have some documents related to that time frame, and if we could -- I just want to show you them very, very briefly. The first is P686, if we could show him I believe should be (B), which is the B/C/S version. And perhaps we can put the English version on the ELMO. It's from the Gazette of the RS regarding strategic objectives. And briefly, Mr. Deronjic, I don't want to go into this document and its history. But can you tell us, is this a genuine document? Were there -- was there a thing called the six strategic objectives? Does this exhibit reflect the true and correct decision?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. This decision, the document that I have in front of me, talks about the strategic objectives of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is dated 1992. And in my statement I talked at some length about this document and when I came to learn about it. The document is a genuine one and it describes political objectives of the leadership of Republika Srpska in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And we do -- the Court does have the synopsis of your statement, so I don't think we need to ask anything further on that point. Now, let me show you what's been marked P687. And you've also, as you know, in your most recent statements to the Prosecutor spoken of your appointment as civilian commissioner. In fact, I think you've spoken about that in most of your statements. Is this document, P687, the actual physical document appointing you as civilian commissioner?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is the document in question. I've already had an opportunity to see him. I had it in my possession, and I handed it over to the Prosecutor. This is the decision on the appointment of myself to the position of civilian commissioner for the Serbian municipality of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When did you first get a -- actually a physical copy of that so you could see what the president had done on paper?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I mentioned in my statement to the Prosecutor that it was on the 11th of July, and I'm referring to the 11th of July of 1995, that I had a conversation with the President. And it was then that he first informed me of my appointment to the position of civilian commissioner. I insisted that he sent me a written copy specifying my functions, although I was already familiar with the institution of civilian commissioner as such. He promised he would send this to me. I believe that there should be a -- in the original document, the date when I actually received it by fax in my office. But I believe it could have been three to four days after my conversation with the President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, just as a matter of procedure, you've prefaced your remarks as you've said to the Office of the Prosecutor. And it's important that when you're answering the questions that you speak directly to those questions to me or to counsel or to the Court, so that we know you're answering the questions directly and you're not just telling us what you told the Prosecutor. I think I understand that as does the Court. But it's for the record and for the process, it's important that we understand that you're speaking today directly to us. All right. And just another document, 688, the appointment to the War Presidency. It's a document you received at the same time. And can you just briefly tell us what this is.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: On the 14th of July, 1995, at a meeting held at Pale, Mr. Karadzic informed me that a decision on the appointment of civilian commissioner is to be renamed, rephrased, and that a War Presidency would be established in the Srebrenica municipality, which was the reason why we met with the representatives of Serbs from Srebrenica. During the afternoon hours of that day, we adopted a decision concerning the composition of the War Presidency for the Srebrenica municipality, whereby I was appointed President of the War Presidency. Whereas, the eight remaining individuals named in this decision were appointed members of this War Presidency. Once again, the decision was reached on the 14th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, could we go into closed session briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in the open session. Mr. Karnavas, do you prefer to start your cross-examination now or we might have an early break? The time is the same allocated to you, I can guarantee you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would prefer that we have a break so the Prosecution could get a chance to hunt down that agreement that was signed back on I believe it's the 18th of June or July, 2003, for me to get set up so I can be most efficient with my time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So we'll resume at 25 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas. Your cross-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before we discuss your background, I thought we would begin with the very first statement that you gave, that was in 16 December, 1997. Do you recall that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And just for the record, when you stated earlier on direct that it was the first meeting that you had back on February 4, 1998, and you gave your explanation as to why you were less than truthful, that wasn't the first statement, in fact that was a second encounter. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the first time that you met with them back in 16 December, 1997, that was in Pale, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you were informed on that occasion that you would be meeting with representatives of the Tribunal, or did they just show up unannounced?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, I was informed about the meeting by Mr. Neskovic. I don't know exactly what his post was in the government of Republika Srpska at the time, but I think I was summoned to the meeting and it was explained to me that I needed to come to Pale and to give a statement to investigators of The Hague Tribunal regarding the events in Srebrenica. And I was told that I was not subject of the investigation at the meeting, but that I should give certain statements -- a statement regarding the circumstances of the participation of Mr. Karadzic since the indictment against him was already issued concerning those events. So Mr. Neskovic informed me and gave me some details about that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now -- and I don't want to get ahead of ourselves, but at this point were you still the vice-president of the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: No. In 1997, before this meeting, I left the majority of the political functions that I had in the SDS until then, and I think that I was not the vice-president of the SDS at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When you were vice-president of the SDS, was Mr. Karadzic the president?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as the president, would that make him the head of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You would be his second in command, in the party that is?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Well, how should I explain that to you? At the time, there was seven vice-presidents, so I was one of those seven vice-presidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We'll get to that later on. In any event, when you also stated today that you were somewhat caught by surprise that you were being summoned back in 1998 to give a statement, is it not kind of odd that you would be surprised, given that you had already met with someone from the Tribunal in December 16, 1997?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I mentioned this meeting in 1998, I said that these were the first meetings with the Tribunal, including this one from 1997. I was somewhat surprised because of those meetings, because I was invited by our government via Mr. Neskovic to come and provide the statement, even though nobody explained in detail the nature of this statement that I was supposed to provide, nor the status that I had vis-a-vis the Tribunal and the investigators. And I believed that perhaps it was necessary for them to give me some questions, and I did ask Mr. Neskovic if I could be provided with some questions so that I could prepare and adequately respond to them. But he said that I should just appear. And then in a conversation with the OTP representatives, we will see what is connected to me and those events and then we will see. So for me it was somewhat of a surprise when Mr. Jean Rene Ruez said that I needed to provide a comprehensive statement about all the events in Srebrenica, including some preparatory actions and all the things -- and how things proceed over those few key days in July 1995. I was not prepared to provide such a comprehensive statement, and I told Mr. Ruez in that conversation that I cannot provide a detailed specific statement because I wasn't prepared for it for such wide -- a broad range of events. And he agreed with that. And I think that is also stated in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Deronjic, one thing I can assure you is that I will be as thorough as I possibly can be with all of your statements, each and every one of them. So I will try to narrow my questions, and if you could narrow your answers to my questions, we might be able to get through this as quickly as possible. Now, getting back to my original question, today you were asked by Mr. McCloskey with respect to your statement dated February 4, 1998. And at that time Mr. McCloskey asked you, and I quote: "Can you briefly explain that, why you were not correctly relating the events when you met with Mr. Ruez?" Okay. That was the question. And then you began to say in your answer that you were surprised -- that this invitation came as a surprise and it was the first such invitation and that it was only then that I realised that I was -- that I was interesting for the investigators of the OTP. And I'm reading from the official transcript that we have. That was your answer. Now, sir, here is my question: If this is February 4, 1998, that would have been your second meeting with the Office of the Prosecution or the Tribunal because you had a previous one, had you not, back in 1997, to be specific, 16 December 1997. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, during that particular meeting you were asked questions and you provided some answers. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in fact before coming here today - and I would guess, given that you had three very competent lawyers, one especially from the United States, very familiar with entering into plea agreements - you had an opportunity to go over all of your statements with your lawyers and for you yourself, knowing that you would be testifying. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, to a large degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'm going to go over in great detail the first statement that you made back on 16th December 1997. But is it not a fact that during that conversation that you had, you informed them that it was a pity, it was a shame that they did not have enough time or you did not have enough time during that occasion and that you wanted to meet with them again in order to give them more detailed information. Do you recall reading that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So in other words, you expected them to come back after you had your first meeting in 1997. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I assumed that there would be more conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You assumed because of the nature of the questioning. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Because of the importance of the events that we had started to discuss.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, not just the importance of the events but also because of your particular role, at least with respect to how you had described it during that questioning process. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. My role was very important in those events, and I assumed that there would be more conversations because of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Correct. And in fact you specifically stated - and for the record this is D92/1 - I'm reading from your statement and it's on page 4 of the English version. But I'll read it to you and if you need to look at the Srpski version I can give you the particular line. But just let me read it and see if it refreshes your -- if I'm correct. You say: "I hope next time you come we have more time to discuss. There are a lot of details which deserve to be explained better. I will be in a position to do so next time." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, one can only assume that after this particular meeting you were fully aware of what sort of preparation you needed to make for the next encounter with the OTP. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So once again, getting back to what you testified earlier today, you were incorrect in stating that during the February 4 meeting you were not only taken by surprise but also you were unaware of the general nature of the discussions, hence your inability of being more precise, and that was one of the reasons that you gave. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, perhaps I didn't understand too precisely about which conversation Mr. McCloskey was asking me about. Perhaps I thought that he was asking me about the first conversation, and perhaps that is why I gave the answer that I did give.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, thank you very much. And incidentally, if there ever comes an occasion where you don't understand me, because I have this habit sometimes as making long questions, please ask me to rephrase. But I'll try to be as specific as possible. All right. Now, if we could get to the very first statement. By the way, do you have a copy of that, because I understand you have some documents with you. Do you have it with you by any chance? And I'm referring to specifically what is titled as Information Report dated 16 December 1997, and again for the record, it's D92/1. Do you have it with you Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I don't have it, Mr. Karnavas. So if you do have a copy, I would be very grateful if you give it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I do have a copy, and I have it in Srpski. Before we get to that, to the actual questioning, you indicated also today that you were somewhat -- perhaps you were less than honest or truthful during that occasion because of the place where the interview took, because you were in Pale, and I believe in an office in the government building. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: May I ask: Who chose that particular venue, OTP or you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Well, I was in no opportunity to pick the venue, so either it was the OTP or somebody from the Republika Srpska leadership chose that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And what about the particular room within the government building? Did you pick it out or did somebody pick it out for you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: No. The office was allocated. I really don't know who allocated the office. Inside they had the technical equipment which helped us to conduct the interview. I'm thinking of the microphones, the cassette tape, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, there was an interpreter there to assist both you and the Prosecution. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was the interpreter one provided by the government of the RS or was that an interpreter that was there on behalf of the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask such questions and I really couldn't give you an answer. They just introduced him to me and asked me if I agreed for him to interpret during the interview, and I agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In any event during that interview you did not at any time indicate that you wanted to have the interview someplace else because you felt uncomfortable?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that at that point, and I think that if I had said something like that at that location, assuming that they were taping, something like that would be also recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Fair to say that subsequent to this occasion when you met with the Prosecution on the other times, you did not feel that same fear. Is that correct? Would that be a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: No. That is not correct. The fear increased to a certain degree, because later I found out that a part or practically all of my interviews and their contents had reached some addresses as a result of which I was very unhappy that they had reached these addresses. And I had warned the Prosecution, Mr. Jean Ruez, at some point. And even during an interview when Mr. Harmon was present, I had the exact information where these interviews were being sent and who was using them and where they were being used, and I warned the Prosecution about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So just to make sure I understand, it's your testimony today that there was a leak in the Office of the Prosecution, and they were somehow -- were passing on your interviews to folks in the community. Is that a correct interpretation of what you're stating?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: No. That is not correct. I didn't say that the Prosecution directed these interviews or provided information to somebody, but simply that there were other ways that these interviews were reaching addresses that they were not supposed to address. But I did have absolutely clear information about how some of my interviews or practically all of my interviews were going where they should not have been going to. But I am not aware of the way in which they got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I just don't want to give up on this point yet. Mr. Deronjic, assuming that the Prosecution was taking these statements and assuming that the members of their team, that is the interpreters, were the only other people in the room while you were being questioned other than your own lawyers, how would it be possible for somebody else to be spreading that information? It would either come from the OTP or it would come from your own lawyers or it might come from you. So either you're accusing the OTP of leaking information or having a mole in the sense of somebody acting as a spy in their office, or maybe there was a leak by way of others participating in this conversation such as your own lawyers or perhaps you yourself. Which one is it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I cannot choose any of the options, but I can provide another one and that is the premises where we were conducting particularly the initial interviews. There were perhaps some bugging or recording devices. I do not know too much about these technical details, but there is that possibility. Secondly, I would like to say that during those initial interviews it's true that I had lawyers. I think, if I remember correctly, they did attend one of the interviews. I had two lawyers, Mr. Neskovic and Mr. Pantelic. They were not my lawyers, but I was told when I got to Pale that I had been provided with two attorneys who can assist me during my giving of the interview. I cannot remember whether they were present at one or two of these meetings, but as I had already understood that some information was already being leaked from those interviews, I, shortly afterwards, refused the assistance of both of those attorneys in order at least to eliminate that particular possible source of the spread of information. And I informed Mr. Ruez that in future I would be coming to the meetings alone. Of course I do not wish to accuse them in any way, because I have no proof that they were the source of this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And of course one of the reasons you were also appearing alone during those interviews while you were still consulting with your lawyers was you wanted to give the appearance that you had nothing to hide, you didn't need a lawyer, and therefore perhaps that would be somewhat persuasive in not eventually charging you. Correct? Just a yes or no would do.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Getting -- now, let's focus on this initial interview. Now, Mr. Deronjic, in your initial interview you indicated that you learned of your appointment as Srebrenica -- when it became clear that Srebrenica would fall. That's on paragraph 3. Do you recall making that statement? It's on the first page, first page, there's no need to turn the page, third paragraph. You indicate that: "I was appointed when it became clear that Srebrenica would fall." My question is: Is that correct, did you learn it when it became apparent that it would fall or had it fallen? Which one is it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I think that the correct answer is when I realised or when it became clear that Srebrenica would fall, as our units were entering Srebrenica -- or rather, while they were moving towards Srebrenica, I received this piece of information. But practically speaking, Srebrenica had not yet fallen at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And so -- at that point you indicate that you first learned of the decision of your appointment through the media. Correct? That's the next line, through the media?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So when you say "media," what are we talking about? Television? Radio? Which media? Newspaper?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: No. I was informed through the police that Karadzic wanted me to get in touch with him as quickly as possible from Bratunac. They took me in a police car to Bratunac, and the police officers in the car told me that the possible reason as to why Karadzic was looking for me was the fact that it was broadcast over the radio that I had been appointed to the position of a civilian commissioner or some other position, I don't exactly recall the name that they gave this position. That's what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So when you say that you "learned it through the media," that was false. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say that it was false? That I personally learned --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you state here, Mr. Deronjic, you state here: "I first learned the decision through the media." That's here. And as we will see, you repeat that on other occasions. And on one occasion I believe you say mass media. Today for the very first time we hear that the police came and got you and then transported you to the Bratunac Brigade headquarters where you could make a phone call and speak directly to the president. So my question to you today is: Is it -- is this not false then when you state that you first learned the decision through the media, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: The -- this is not false because I learned it through the media indirectly. It was the police and the people I encountered who told me that this piece of information had been broadcast over the media. But I learned about it directly from the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So the police heard it, and they decided on their own, we better go search for Deronjic. He might be somewhere on the front line, our president of the SDS. And that's how they went and found you and they transported you back to the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I don't understand why you are misinterpreting my answer. Someone was informed that the president was looking for me, that he wanted to see me. This was conveyed to the police, and it was the police that looked for me and got me. And the chief of the public security station probably responded, and he called his men at the Pribicevac post by Motorola and informed them that they should get me and bring me to President Karadzic, who wanted to see me. So it was not those police officers who decided on their own to get me and to bring me to the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Why didn't you give this explanation back then when you were being questioned? It seems somewhat innocuous, nothing to worry about, about how you learned of your appointment?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Well, I must admit that it is rather difficult to provide detailed explanation for everything. I perhaps didn't deem it to be very important as to who it was who first heard it on the radio and who informed me of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. In any event, you state that you asked for -- you did speak with President Karadzic at some point -- and you asked for a meeting. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I talked to President Karadzic in the evening of the 11th of July. I talked to him on the telephone from the brigade headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And then you state that: "We met I think one day after." That's what you state. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So if you met with him one day after, that would have been in July 12th?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: If I met with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What do you mean if you met with him? You either met with him or you did not meet with him.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't meet with him. That's exactly where the problem is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So you did not meet with him on the 11th?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And again I don't want to get ahead of myself, but do you recall giving a statement at some other point in time where you indicated that on that particular day, July 11th, 1995, you in fact drove to Pale and spoke directly with President Karadzic. Do you recall making that statement?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recall making that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So I take it that statement, when you made it, was knowingly false?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't call it knowingly false. Those were my first statements, my first, my second, and my third statement concerning these events. And frankly, at that time it was difficult for me to remember all those events. I did as best as I could. And as you can see from these statements, I often warned the Prosecution of my insecurity with respect to the dates. I checked the dates later on and I'm sure you will realise how difficult it is to remember particular dates, dates of the meetings, the exact hours and so on and so forth. This is what I had to do on my own. I had to refresh my memory of those years, and if you read carefully my statements, you will see that with every subsequent statement, the dates and the hours are more precise, the dates of meetings and various encounters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Suffice it to say, Mr. Deronjic, that you are -- again, I don't want to get ahead of myself, but you are a student of literature, correct, of the language?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You have a degree in that. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You were a teacher. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So you understand all about linguistic nuances. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, getting back to what you just stated, Srebrenica, the falling of Srebrenica, was a historic occasion during those days, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There is no doubt in your mind that Srebrenica fell in fact on 11 July 1995. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You don't need to look at some notebook or some diary or ask some neighbour when Srebrenica fell, because of your particular position and because of the momentous occasion of the falling of Srebrenica, you know that it was July 11, 1995. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you -- let us not enter into a debate as to the limits of the memory. Unfortunately Srebrenica was not the only event that attracted my attention. Obviously it was the most important one, but there was a number of other events taking place at the time. 13 to 1400 were killed -- people were killed in Bratunac, and I expressed my condolences to all those families. So all of these events occupy my memory. Some are clear and precise in my mind and some are not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, is the event of the falling of Srebrenica clear in your mind, or are you having some difficulty recounting the events as they occurred during those days?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe you asked this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll withdraw and move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now -- so it's your firm testimony today that on the 11th of July 1995, you did not in fact go to Pale to meet with President Karadzic, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you then go on to state that one of the reasons that you met with -- you spoke with President Karadzic was because you wanted to have clear guidance as to what your specific role was going to be as the commissioner of Srebrenica. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And when you gave this statement, you indicated that it was President Karadzic who told you that you, that is Miroslav Deronjic, was directly responsible to the president in order to assist in -- to take care of the citizens of Srebrenica. Do you recall making that statement?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. This concerned directly the issue of providing assistance in terms of securing accommodation for the civilians after the military operation in Srebrenica, that that was what I was in charge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But the civilians meant not just the Serb civilians that were in Bratunac or in other places that wanted to get back to their homes in Srebrenica, but also the civilians from Srebrenica - and I'm talking specifically the Muslims - who had left Srebrenica and now were in Potocari. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So was that statement accurate, that is that you, Miroslav Deronjic, the President of the SDS for the Bratunac municipality, now also wearing the hat of commissioner of Srebrenica, was ordered to -- by the President to be responsible in taking care of the civilians, both Serb and Muslim. Was that a correct statement?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So in other words you, by this admission at least today, would be responsible for the events that occurred subsequent to the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: What events do you have in mind, concerning civilians or events generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Concerning civilians and the events that took place, and we don't have to get into a long debate about the events because I'm sure you know them better than I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That's vague. There are a lot of events and he can't possibly be responsible for all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll rephrase, Your Honour. I'll rephrase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Given your position, given your position, are you not responsible for the events as they related to the civilians of Srebrenica, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again, objection. That is extremely vague. Again, even defining civilians can be a difficult task, so that is not a helpful question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas, please try to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, when I'm referring to civilians I'm saying non-military personnel, such as, if the Prosecutor wishes me to be specific, the men that were separated from the women and children and ultimately were massacred.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Are you not responsible for those events, since you were given by the president of the RS that responsibility, in your capacity as the highest official in Bratunac at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I must admit that you have confused me with a rather complex question, containing a number of implications. You say that Mr. Karadzic had tasked me with the treatment of civilians in Srebrenica because he had information and I had information that the civilians had separated from the military forces, the Srebrenica Muslims, and had gathered around the UN compound in Potocari. When we discussed it around the 11th, my task -- he said that my task would be the treatment of the civilians who gathered there. And he gave me precise instructions as to what I should do in order to fulfill this role that I had. He said that I should invite or make contact with all relevant entities in Bratunac at the moment, the police, the military, the international forces, and that all together we should establish contact with the representatives of the Srebrenica Muslims. And he told me clearly what it was that I should convey to them at the meeting. This included three options as regards the fate of those civilians. And let me finish. Among other things, the treatment of any potential prisoners of war who might use this opportunity to shelter themselves or to join this group of civilians, the order, the specific order, was that those men should be retained. And this is what I conveyed at the meeting in the Fontana Hotel with all the relevant entities who happened to be in the field at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Deronjic, and we're going to get to that. But if I can refer to one of the documents that was introduced today. And I'm preferring to P687, and this is the decision appointing you as a civilian commissioner for the Serbian municipality of Srebrenica. If you could look at that document. I believe yours would be B, 687/B. Since this was introduced today, I guess I can forego the foundational formalities. You do recognise this document, do you not, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And am I correct in stating that in fact you had provided this document to the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I take it that you have had an opportunity to read it and read it carefully, have you not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could draw your attention now to paragraph number 4. If you could please read it to yourself first, and then we will read it together jointly piece by piece.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I am familiar with this. I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, does it not state, Mr. Deronjic, that the commissioner, that being Miroslav Deronjic, shall ensure that all civilian and military organs treat all civilians who participated in combat against the Army of Republika Srpska as prisoners of war and ensure that the civilian population can freely choose where they will live or move to." Does it not state that? Does it not state that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. The word "shall" means that you are mandated, that you are required; it's not optional. Correct? Am I correct? We need to make a record, Mr. Deronjic. You must speak up so we can record your answer for the record.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: That's exactly what it says, and I agree that that's what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And ensure means shall ensure, you know, that you have this responsibility. Right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. That "all civilian and military organs," and by that we're talking civilian such as the special police; and military organs such as the VRS units. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I assume that that's what it means, that there was no other army there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. "That they treat all citizens who participated in combat against the Army of the Republika Srpska as prisoners of war." Now, by that, by "all citizens," does this not mean that -- does this not include those who were combatant from the age of 16 to 60, as was the case that was singled out during those days after the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: That's what follows from this wording.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I understand that it follows, but I want to a commitment from you that that is your understanding to make sure that we are on the same page, that we're talking about civilians -- when it talks about citizens, it also refers to military personnel of the Muslim army. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: If I can kindly ask you to finish your questions with respect of this, and then I will give you my answer. But let me just remind you of the fact that I did not have this document on the 12th when the meeting at Fontana was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's not -- well, first, let's focus on what we're doing here. And I'm breaking the questions down for the record, lest there be any complaints from the Prosecution that I'm making compound questions and confusing you. So when I talk about all civilians, this all civilians includes men of military age, Muslims from Srebrenica. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: All civilians include men of military age, so I don't really understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, my question here, in particular, specifically, apparently there must have been a reason for President Karadzic, he highlights and he says, "Who participated in combat against the Army of Republika Srpska." So by that, can we not agree, sir, that there can be no confusion that the word "citizens" includes military personnel?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. It follows from this text that citizens, the word "citizens" also includes men of military age.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And when it said that they are to be treated as prisoners of war, does it not mean that they should be accorded all of the rights and protections given to prisoners of war as were required at the time under the Geneva Conventions. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So getting back to my earlier question, the one that was rather confusing that drew an objection, would it not be fair to say that you, given your position, it had been given to you from President Karadzic during those days, you were responsible for the well being of all the citizens from Srebrenica who had gathered in Potocari. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: It would be correct, provided that I had this document with precise instructions at the time we were carrying out the instructions given by Karadzic. However, those instructions were conveyed to me orally on the 11th, and they did not contain these specific references. And I carried out those instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, we're going to get to all of that, and we will see whether you had this or not. But my question is: Based on this document, does it not put you responsible for the well being of all of those citizens from Srebrenica that had gathered at Potocari. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And if we were to take this paragraph and read it literally, it would also mean, would it not, that you were also responsible for the well being of all of the Muslim soldiers that had left in the column but later on were captured. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Theoretically speaking, yes, one could say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when we say "theoretically," that's how -- this document is a legal document, is it not? It has lawful significance, did it not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. So it's not in theory, it's in fact. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, the main facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we were to look at paragraph 5, and I think this is why you might have qualified your answer as theoretically, if we look at paragraph 5, the next paragraph, it does state that your particular decisions "shall be binding for all civilian authority organs in the Serbian municipality of Srebrenica." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so I can only imagine that when you said "theoretically," what you meant was you as the commissioner perhaps did not have authority over the military organs. That is, your decisions were not binding on the military organs. Is that correct? Is that what you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: That and many other things. Of course that is one of the first things -- facts that I wanted to point to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, to the extent that I can, I'm going to try to forecast what your concerns might be. But even if we look at paragraph 5, going back to paragraph 4, we must agree, must we not, that even though your decisions may not be binding on the military, nonetheless by virtue of paragraph 4 you are ultimately responsible for the well being of all of those people that were there in Potocari and the soldiers, the Muslim soldiers that were captured during those days. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, getting back to -- well, getting back to my initial question. Then is it not fair to conclude that you would, by virtue of the admissions that you have just made to my questions and based on the document that you provided to the Prosecution, a document I am sure had quite a significance during that period of time, isn't it a fact that you would be responsible then for any harm that had come to those civilians during those days?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. You have drawn a fantastic conclusion. Let me just say something. This is not about my responsibility, and I do not view it in that way. So I am stating facts and it doesn't matter what they signify. It's up to the Trial Chamber to determine whether I have some responsibility or not. This is the first thing I want to say. The second thing is that I was acting in accordance with oral instructions or orders I received from President Karadzic, which I received at the command. So these -- the only information -- this is the only information that I had from a meeting which I attended, which was on the 12th at the Hotel Fontana. But up until that time I had no other instructions, even though I asked President Karadzic to send me more instructions. Had I even had such instructions, it would mean that I was being given a role above that of General Mladic by Mr. Karadzic, and if anybody could draw the conclusion that I as a lower-ranking party official was in a position to command General Mladic, and if that is accepted by others I would accept it, too. But this has no logic at all. The meeting I explained in detail. The majority of the conversations from that meeting, transcripts exist at this Tribunal, and from them it's evident how I acted in accordance with President Karadzic's instructions, what General Mladic did when he took over responsibility for the fates of those civilians and what did I do to help for those civilians to leave Bratunac in a safe way. At the end, I just wanted to say the following: You know, probably you are aware that in front of this Tribunal de facto and de jure responsibility of certain participants in certain events is being established. And sometimes the de facto role can be more important than the de jure function and the other way around. If you need broader explanations, of course I can provide them. But in principle what I am saying is that we are not establishing my responsibility here. I am just stating the facts, no matter what their meaning is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, let me just be more direct then. Mr. Deronjic, do you hold yourself criminally liable, responsible, for any of the events that happen in 1995, in July 1995, from the period of, say, the 11th after the fall of Srebrenica to, say, up until the period where the mass graves were reburied and relocated? Do you hold yourself responsible for any of that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: You know, Mr. Karnavas, I had the opportunity during this long period to think over each detail. I put in a systemic way some of the common points between myself and the events in Srebrenica from that period. And these are things where this mutual connection can be boiled down to about 15 points, no matter how objective or subjective I can be, you can take it as you wish. I personally, however, cannot state my position in regard to that question, and I'm leaving it up to the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution to make their conclusions on that. I am leaving it up to the Prosecution after all the investigations, and this was something that was told -- that I was told after all the investigations were completed, that indictments in relation to Srebrenica were being dropped against me. But even the direct question of the President of the Trial Chamber which questioned me to a direct question, the Prosecution stated that there is no direct responsibility on my part for those events and that they have no intention of prosecuting me further for the events in Srebrenica. I would like to stop now because I could be understood subjectively in this or that way. I am leaving it up to time also which will augment the things that I have stated once the whole truth is discovered, and I think this will prove favourable to me once the whole truth is presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Deronjic, before we go further on this information report, let's touch upon a little bit on the agreement you've reached with the Prosecution. Is it not a fact that in essence you have amnesty from the Prosecution for any of your conduct with respect to the events in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are not aware of any factual basis for that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas, would you please lay some ground for that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour, and I don't wish to get into a debate with Mr. McCloskey, but I would appreciate if we could have answers from the Prosecutor -- I mean from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may ask some questions in this aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, you entered into an agreement with the Prosecution at some point, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, initially you had entered -- you signed an understanding of the parties dated 18 June 2003. Correct? That was after your arrest.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me walk you down the events as they occurred prior to that. You first -- your first contact with the Office of the Prosecution or this Tribunal was 16 December 1997. That's the one that we're discussing; that's the one in Pale. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct. I've already stated several times that that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Then you gave a statement, again as a witness, on 4 February 1998. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Then on July 1st, 1998, you met with the Office of the Prosecution; a statement was not given at that time. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the date again. I'm sorry, I didn't register the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: July 1, 1998. You did not provide a statement during your meeting with Mr. Ruez on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: It's possible. I cannot remember that 100 per cent, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That particular occasion was the one, if I may refresh your memory, where you were formally informed that your status had changed from witness to suspect. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now -- again, not to get ahead of myself, on that particular occasion, upon learning that your status had changed, you requested for Mr. Ruez to provide you what areas, what elements, or what portions of your previous statement specifically were relevant to your changing of the -- your status change from witness to suspect. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And of course you were -- if we were to go to the statement, and I have it here. If we were to go to the statement, we would find, would we not, that you insisted that you be told by Mr. Ruez what specific points in your previous statement were relevant to the changing of your status?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And of course Mr. Ruez was not accommodating. He was friendly but not accommodating. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I think that he was not, and I think I understand why he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well -- but the answer is: He was not willing to give you any specific reasons as to why your status had changed. Right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And of course it might have been because he did not want you then to go back and perhaps try to figure out what explanations you might be able to come up for those relevant points that had changed your status. Right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: He wanted me to find an explanation, that's why I asked him. Unless you think that that's giving me an opportunity to conceal something. Perhaps that could have been the motive why he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And in fact during that meeting, it ended with your lawyer who was present -- you had two lawyers present during that day, but one of them who was acting as a consultant, he requested that the OTP would provide you with all of the relevant documents so you could have -- in order so the next occasion when you would be more forthcoming, you would be able to be more helpful with more details?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And is it not correct, sir, to state that at that time the whole focus of the questioning of the Office of the Prosecution was on Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Srebrenica was in 1995; right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, in your indictment, as we will see later on, there is nothing there, not one iota with respect to the counts relevant to the events of Srebrenica, is there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Well, I did not write my own indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I am thinking that you would probably compose it differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I'm a Defence lawyer, so perhaps. But needless to say, your indictment, the initial one, that's dated 3 July 2002 is related only to the events of 1992 commonly known as Glogova. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And yet prior to your indictment and subsequent to the time that you were declared a suspect in July 1, 1998, you gave a statement on 21 October 1999, that being your fourth statement or the fourth meeting. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Before the indictment was issued, yes, I did provide more statement, and of course that one was before the indictment was issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you gave another statement on 21 March 2001; that was your fifth encounter with the Prosecution. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not quite sure about the number of them, so I'm not sure whether that is how it goes in the chronological order, but I assume that it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And then we have one dated April 2002, and then the indictment. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in fact, it's not until you meet with the Prosecution for the last couple of times that the issue of Glogova and your involvement is really discussed at any detail?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: No. I think that Mr. Ruez and I covered the questions relating to 1992 in an earlier interview, and he told me then that he would not really be going into the details of those events and that there will be another team that will be investigating 1992 and that I would be called in for those interviews for certain. So this was already the second statement relating to the events in Glogova, and it was more detailed and broader and it encompassed all of the events outside of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to clarify. The meeting of March 2001 was on the 12th of March, just for the record. I think you just reversed the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, according to my reading of the statements, Mr. Deronjic, it would appear that Glogova first comes into the picture in any real significance during your statement given on 8 April 2002, that being the sixth encounter with the Prosecution, the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: It appeared before. I don't know now to what extent, but I think that we discussed Glogova in detail during a previous interview. But the most serious conversations or interviews from that -- of that period are from that date, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But in any event, is it not a fair characterisation that the Prosecution focused initially on your involvement in Srebrenica. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in fact, if we were to look at all of your statements, would it not be correct to state that that is the primary and predominant importance of your statements, that is, Srebrenica and not Glogova?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is asking him to speculate --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
